name: Chief Bastion
description: Chief Bastion is a stern, imposing world of grey mountains and amber dust seas that stretch to every horizon between the ranges. The planet's largest mountain chain rises nearly twenty kilometers above the mean surface level, its peaks so high they pierce the thin atmosphere into near-vacuum. An ancient meteor crater in the southern hemisphere spans four hundred kilometers and has filled over geological time with fine crystalline dust that sparkles like crushed diamond in direct sunlight.

The thin atmosphere strips away warmth rapidly after sunset, plunging the surface from tolerable to lethal cold within hours. Days are quiet and bright, the sky a deep indigo that darkens to black at the zenith where stars are visible even at noon. The dust seas shift in the wind with a whispering sound, and occasional dust devils rise in silent columns that can reach kilometers in height before dissipating.

Ancient ruins discovered in the crystal caverns beneath the main mountain range predate any known civilization by at least a hundred thousand years. The ruins' architectural style is austere and monumental, carved directly from the mountain's crystalline substrate with tools that left no identifiable marks. Deep-penetrating radar has revealed a megastructure beneath the ruins that extends far below the planet's crust, its lowest detectable levels approaching the mantle boundary. Microbial life thrives in the caverns around the structure's upper surfaces, feeding on mineral seepage and faint thermal emissions.

Chief Bastion's platinum and dark crystal deposits make it commercially interesting, but the xenoarchaeological significance of the ruins and megastructure has placed the entire mountain range under protective jurisdiction. Unauthorized excavation carries severe penalties, though the remoteness of the world makes enforcement challenging. The megastructure emits a low-frequency vibration detectable only by seismic instruments, and its frequency has shifted twice in the last decade, leading some researchers to believe it is not merely an artifact but an active system.
